n: After Hezekiah’s faithful reforms, Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah (701 BC) and besieged its fortified cities. Faithfulness doesn’t exempt us from trials, but it prepares us for them.

f.g: Ruled Assyria about 705–681 BC; his own annals boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem ‘like a bird in a cage.’

n: Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib intended to attack Jerusalem itself.
With his officials and warriors, he decided to block the springs outside the city, and they supported him.

f.g: Cover or divert the springs so the enemy would lack water.

n: Many people helped seal the springs and the stream, asking, “Why should Assyria’s kings find plenty of water?”

f.w: the brook that ran through the midst of the land
f.g: Probably the stream flowing from the Gihon spring in the Kidron Valley.

n: Hezekiah rebuilt the broken wall, raised towers, built a second outer wall, reinforced the Millo, and made many weapons. Faith and preparation work together.

f.g: Archaeologists have found a thick wall in Jerusalem dated to Hezekiah’s time, the ‘Broad Wall.’
Terraced fortifications in the City of David.
Spears or javelins.

n: He appointed commanders and gathered the people in the square at the city gate to encourage them.

f.g: Spoke encouragingly — literally ‘to their heart.’

n: Be strong and courageous; don’t fear Assyria’s king or his army, for there are more with us than with him — words echoing Elisha’s vision of heavenly armies.

f.w: there be more with us than with him

n: “With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God.” Human power versus divine help — the people were steadied by these words.

f.g: Merely human strength.
Relied on; took confidence from.

n: While Sennacherib besieged Lachish with his main army, he sent officials to Jerusalem with a message for Hezekiah and the people.

f.g: Sennacherib’s siege of Lachish is pictured in stone reliefs from his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum.

n: Sennacherib’s message: “What are you trusting in, to stay under siege in Jerusalem?” He tried to undermine their faith.
Isn’t Hezekiah deceiving you into dying of hunger and thirst by claiming the Lord will save you?

f.g: Mislead; incite.

n: He twisted Hezekiah’s reforms into an insult: hasn’t Hezekiah removed the Lord’s own shrines and told you to worship at only one altar? The Assyrians misunderstood that this was obedience, not disrespect.
Don’t you know what my ancestors and I have done to other nations? Their gods couldn’t save them.
Which god of any nation we destroyed could rescue his people? How then could yours?

f.g: Completely devoted to destruction.

n: Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you. No god has stopped us — how much less will your God! His mistake was to treat the living God like a lifeless idol.

f.w: how much less shall your God deliver you

n: His officials said even more against the Lord God and His servant Hezekiah.
Sennacherib also wrote letters mocking the God of Israel, insisting He could no more save His people than the other gods.

f.g: To insult; to taunt.

n: They shouted in Hebrew to the people on the walls to frighten and demoralize them so the city would surrender.

f.g: In Hebrew, the people’s language, rather than the diplomatic Aramaic.
To terrify them.

n: They spoke of Jerusalem’s God as if He were one of the man-made gods of the nations. That was their fatal error.

f.w: the work of the hands of man

n: So King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah prayed and cried out to heaven. King and prophet united in prayer.

f.w: the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz

n: The Lord sent an angel who destroyed the Assyrian warriors and commanders. Sennacherib went home in disgrace, and later his own sons killed him in his god’s temple.

f.g: 2 Kings 19:35 records 185,000 Assyrians slain in one night.

f.w: they that came forth of his own bowels slew him
f.g: His own sons murdered him (681 BC).

n: So the Lord saved Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Sennacherib and all others, and gave them rest on every side.

f.g: Or ‘gave them rest all around.’

n: Many brought offerings to the Lord and gifts to Hezekiah, and he became highly respected among the nations.

f.g: Exalted; held in high honor.

n: Around this time Hezekiah became deathly ill. He prayed, and the Lord answered and gave him a sign — the shadow moving backward on the sundial — adding fifteen years to his life.
But Hezekiah didn’t respond with proper gratitude; his heart became proud, bringing God’s displeasure on him and Judah. Even the faithful can stumble after great blessings.

f.w: rendered not again according to the benefit
f.g: Did not respond in gratitude for the kindness shown him.

n: Then Hezekiah and Jerusalem humbled themselves over their pride, so God’s anger didn’t come in his lifetime.
Hezekiah had great wealth and honor and built treasuries for silver, gold, gems, spices, shields, and valuables.

f.g: Desirable, precious objects.

n: He also built storehouses for grain, wine, and oil, and stalls and pens for livestock.

f.g: Sheepfolds or pens.

n: He acquired towns and large flocks and herds, for God had given him great wealth.
Hezekiah blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channeled the water down to the west side of the City of David — the famous tunnel through solid rock, still walkable in Jerusalem today.

f.g: Hezekiah’s Tunnel, about 1,750 feet (533 m) long, carved to bring water to the Pool of Siloam; an ancient Hebrew inscription inside describes its completion.

n: When Babylonian envoys came to ask about the miracle, God left Hezekiah to himself to test him and reveal what was in his heart. He proudly showed them all his treasures.

f.w: the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon
to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart

n: Hezekiah’s other acts and his good deeds are recorded in the vision of Isaiah and in the book of the kings.

f.w: the vision of Isaiah the prophet

n: Hezekiah was buried with great honor in the upper section of the royal tombs, mourned by all Judah. His son Manasseh succeeded him.

f.g: The highest or most honored place among the royal tombs.
